mn44:1.2: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Sanctuary.
mn44:1.3: Then the lay follower Visākha went to the bhikkhuni Dhammadinnā, and after paying homage to her, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, he asked:
mn44:2.2: What is called embodiment by the Blessed One?’
mn44:2.3: ‘Friend Visākha, these five aggregates affected by clinging are called embodiment by the Blessed One,
mn44:2.4: that is to say: the form aggregate affected by clinging, the feeling aggregate affected by clinging, the perception aggregate affected by clinging, the formations aggregate affected by clinging, the consciousness aggregate affected by clinging.
mn44:2.5: These five aggregates affected by clinging are called embodiment by the Blessed One.’
mn44:2.6: Saying ‘Good, lady’, the lay follower Visākha delighted in the bhikkhuni Dhammadinnā’s words, and after agreeing, he asked her a further question:
mn44:3.1: ‘Lady, “Origin of embodiment, origin of embodiment” is said.
mn44:3.2: What is called the origin of embodiment by the Blessed One?’
mn44:3.3: ‘Friend Visākha, it is that craving which renews being and is accompanied by delight and lust, and delights in this and that, that is to say:
mn44:3.4: craving for sensual desires, craving for being, craving for non-being;
mn44:3.5: this is called the origin of embodiment by the Blessed One.’
mn44:4.1: ‘Lady, “Cessation of embodiment, cessation of embodiment” is said.
mn44:4.2: What is called the cessation of embodiment by the Blessed One?’
mn44:4.3: ‘Friend Visākha, it is the remainderless fading and ceasing, the giving up, relinquishing, letting go and rejecting, of that same craving;
mn44:4.4: this is called cessation of embodiment by the Blessed One.’
mn44:5.1: ‘Lady, “The way leading to the cessation of embodiment, the way leading to the cessation of embodiment” is said.
mn44:5.2: What is called the way leading to the cessation of embodiment by the Blessed One?’
mn44:5.3: ‘Friend Visākha, it is this Noble Eightfold Path, that is to say:
mn44:5.4: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration.’
mn44:6.1: ‘Lady, is that clinging the same as these five aggregates affected by clinging, or is the clinging something apart from these five aggregates affected by clinging?’
mn44:6.2: ‘Friend Visākha, that clinging is neither the same as these five aggregates affected by clinging nor is it something apart from these five aggregates affected by clinging.
mn44:6.3: It is the desire and lust comprised in these five aggregates affected by clinging that is the clinging there.’
mn44:7.1: ‘Lady, how does there come to be the embodiment view?’
mn44:7.2: ‘Here, friend Visākha, the untaught ordinary man who has no regard for the Noble Ones and is unconversant with their Dhamma and undisciplined in it, who has no regard for True Men and is unconversant with their Dhamma and undisciplined in it,
mn44:7.3: sees form as self, or self as possessed of form, or form in self, or self in form.
mn44:7.4: He sees feeling as self, or self as possessed of feeling, or feeling in self, or self in feeling.
mn44:7.5: He sees perception as self, or self as possessed of perception, or perception in self, or self in perception.
mn44:7.6: He sees formations as self, or self as possessed of formations, or formations in self, or self in formations.
mn44:7.7: He sees consciousness as self, or self as possessed of consciousness, or consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.
mn44:7.8: That is how there comes to be the embodiment view.’
mn44:8.1: ‘Lady, how does there not come to be the embodiment view?’
mn44:8.2: ‘Here, friend Visākha, the well-taught Noble disciple who has regard for Noble Ones and is conversant with their Dhamma and disciplined in it, who has regard for True Men and is conversant with their Dhamma and disciplined in it,
mn44:8.3: does not see form as self, or self as possessed of form, or form in self, or self in form.
mn44:8.4: He does not see feeling as self, or self as possessed of feeling, or feeling in self, or self in feeling.
mn44:8.5: He does not see perception as self, or self as possessed of perception, or perception in self, or self in perception.
mn44:8.6: He does not see formations as self, or self as possessed of formations, or formations in self, or self in formations.
mn44:8.7: He does not see consciousness as self, or self as possessed of consciousness, or consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.
mn44:8.8: That is how there does not come to be the embodiment view.’
mn44:9.1: ‘Lady, what is the Noble Eightfold Path?’
mn44:9.2: ‘Friend Visākha, it is just this Noble Eightfold Path, namely:
mn44:9.3: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration.’
mn44:10.1: ‘Lady, is the Noble Eightfold Path conditioned or unconditioned[^1]?’
mn44:10.2: ‘Friend Visākha, the Noble Eightfold Path is conditioned.’
mn44:11.1: ‘Are the three groups included by the Noble Eightfold Path, lady, or is the Noble Eightfold Path included by the three groups?’
mn44:11.2: ‘The three groups are not included by the Noble Eightfold Path, friend Visākha, but the Noble Eightfold Path is included by the three groups.
mn44:11.3: Any right speech, any right action, any right livelihood: these dhammas are included in the Virtue group.
mn44:11.4: Any right effort, any right mindfulness, any right concentration: these dhammas are included in the Concentration group.
mn44:11.5: Any right view, any right intention: these dhammas are included in the Understanding group.’
mn44:12.1: ‘What is concentration, lady, what is the sign of concentration, what is the equipment of concentration, what is the development of concentration?’
mn44:12.2: ‘Any unification of mind is concentration, friend Visākha;
mn44:12.3: the four foundations of mindfulness are the sign of concentration;
mn44:12.4: the four right endeavours are the equipment of concentration;
mn44:12.5: the repetition, development, and cultivation of those same dhammas are the development of concentration therein.’
mn44:13.2: ‘There are these three processes, friend Visākha:
mn44:13.3: bodily process, verbal process, and mental process.’
mn44:14.1: ‘But, lady, what is a bodily process, what is a verbal process, what is a mental process?’
mn44:14.2: ‘In-breaths and out-breaths are a bodily process, friend Visākha, thinking and exploring[^3] are a verbal process, perception and feeling are a mental process.’
mn44:15.1: ‘But, why are in-breaths and out-breaths a bodily process, lady, why are thinking and exploring a verbal process, why are perception and feeling a mental process?’
mn44:15.2: ‘Friend Visākha, in-breaths and out-breaths belong to a body; these are dhammas bound up with a body, that is why in-breaths and out-breaths are a bodily process.
mn44:15.3: Having previously thought and explored, subsequently one breaks into speech, that is why thinking and exploring are a verbal process.
mn44:15.4: Perception and feeling belong to mind; these are dhammas bound up with mind, that is why perception and feeling are a mental process.’
mn44:16.1: ‘Lady, how does there come to be the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling?’
mn44:16.2: ‘Friend Visākha, when a bhikkhu is attaining cessation of perception and feeling, it does not occur to him:
mn44:16.3: “I shall attain the cessation of perception and feeling” or “I am attaining the cessation of perception and feeling”;
mn44:16.4: but rather his mind has previously been developed in such wise that it induces that state.’
mn44:17.1: ‘Lady, when a bhikkhu is attaining the cessation of perception and feeling, which dhammas come first in him: the bodily process or the verbal process or the mental process?’
mn44:17.2: ‘Friend Visākha, when a bhikkhu is attaining the cessation of perception and feeling, first his verbal process ceases, then his bodily process, then his mental process.’
mn44:18.1: ‘Lady, how does there come to be emergence from the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling?’
mn44:18.2: ‘Friend Visākha, when a bhikkhu is emerging from the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling, it does not occur to him:
mn44:18.3: “I shall emerge from the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling” or “I am emerging from the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling” or “I have emerged from the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling”;
mn44:18.4: but rather his mind has previously been developed in such wise that it induces that state.’
mn44:19.1: ‘Lady, when a bhikkhu is emerging from the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling, which dhammas arise first in him: the bodily process or the verbal process or the mental process?’
mn44:19.2: ‘Friend Visākha, when a bhikkhu is emerging from the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling, first his mental process arises, then his bodily process, then his verbal process.’
mn44:20.1: ‘Lady, when a bhikkhu has emerged from attainment of cessation of perception and feeling, how many kinds of contact touch him?’
mn44:20.2: ‘Friend Visākha, when a bhikkhu has emerged from the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling, three kinds of contact touch him: void contact, signless contact and desireless contact.’
mn44:21.1: ‘Lady, when a bhikkhu has emerged from the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling, to what does his mind incline, lean and tend?’
mn44:21.2: ‘Friend Visākha, when a bhikkhu has emerged from the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling, his mind inclines, leans and tends to seclusion.’
mn44:22.1: ‘Lady, how many kinds of feeling are there?’
mn44:22.2: ‘Friend Visākha, there are three kinds of feeling:
mn44:22.3: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.’
mn44:23.1: ‘But, lady, what is pleasant feeling, what is painful feeling, what is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?’
mn44:23.2: ‘Friend Visākha, whatever is bodily or mentally felt as pleasant and gratifying—
mn44:23.4: Whatever is bodily or mentally felt as painful and hurting—
mn44:23.6: Whatever is bodily or mentally felt as neither gratifying nor hurting—
mn44:24.1: ‘Lady, what is pleasant feeling pleasant in virtue of and painful in virtue of? What is painful feeling painful in virtue of and pleasant in virtue of? What is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling pleasant in virtue of and painful in virtue of?’
mn44:24.2: ‘Friend Visākha, pleasant feeling is pleasant in virtue of presence and painful in virtue of change;
mn44:24.3: painful feeling is painful in virtue of presence and pleasant in virtue of change;
mn44:24.4: neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is pleasant in virtue of knowledge (of it) and painful in virtue of want of knowledge (of it).’
mn44:25.1: ‘Lady, the underlying tendency to what underlies in the case of pleasant feeling? The underlying tendency to what underlies in the case of painful feeling? The underlying tendency to what underlies in the case of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?’
mn44:25.2: ‘Friend Visākha, the underlying tendency to lust underlies in the case of pleasant feeling. The underlying tendency to resistance underlies in the case of painful feeling. The underlying tendency to ignorance underlies in the case of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.’
mn44:26.1: ‘Lady, does the underlying tendency to lust underlie in the case of all pleasant feeling? Does the underlying tendency to resistance underlie in the case of all painful feeling? Does the underlying tendency to ignorance underlie in the case of all neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?’
mn44:26.2: ‘Friend Visākha, the underlying tendency to lust does not underlie in the case of all pleasant feeling. The underlying tendency to resistance does not underlie in the case of all painful feeling. The underlying tendency of ignorance does not underlie in the case of all neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.’
mn44:27.1: ‘Lady, what is abandonable in the case of pleasant feeling? What is abandonable in the case of painful feeling? What is abandonable in the case of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?’
mn44:27.2: ‘Friend Visākha, the underlying tendency to lust is abandonable in the case of pleasant feeling. The underlying tendency to resistance is abandonable in the case of painful feeling. The underlying tendency to ignorance is abandonable in the case of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.’
mn44:28.1: ‘Is the underlying tendency to lust (there and) abandonable in the case of all pleasant feeling? Is the underlying tendency to resistance (there and) abandonable in the case of all painful feeling? Is the underlying tendency to ignorance (there and) abandonable in the case of all neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?’
mn44:28.2: ‘Friend Visākha, it is not in the case of all pleasant feeling that the underlying tendency to lust is there (and so) abandonable, it is not in the case of all painful feeling that the underlying tendency to resistance is there (and so) abandonable, it is not in the case of all neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling that the underlying tendency to ignorance is there (and so) abandonable.
mn44:28.3: ‘Here, quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unprofitable dhammas, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial application and sustained application, with happiness and pleasure born of seclusion:
mn44:28.4: with that he abandons lust, and no underlying tendency to lust underlies that.
mn44:28.6: “When shall I enter upon and abide in that base which Noble Ones now enter upon and abide in?”
mn44:28.7: And as he builds up love for the supreme liberations in this way, grief arises with that love as its condition:
mn44:28.8: with that he abandons resistance, and no underlying tendency to resistance underlies that.
mn44:28.9: ‘Here with the abandoning of pleasure and pain and with the previous disappearance of mental joy and grief, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the fourth jhāna which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity:
mn44:28.10: with that he abandons ignorance, and the underlying tendency to ignorance does not underlie that.’
mn44:29.1: ‘What is a counterpart of pleasant feeling, lady?’
mn44:29.2: ‘Friend Visākha, painful feeling is a counterpart of pleasant feeling.’
mn44:29.3: ‘What is a counterpart of painful feeling, lady?’
mn44:29.4: ‘Friend Visākha, pleasant feeling is a counterpart of painful feeling.’
mn44:29.5: ‘What is a counterpart of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, lady?’
mn44:29.6: ‘Friend Visākha, ignorance is a counterpart of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.’
mn44:29.7: ‘What is a counterpart of ignorance, lady?’
mn44:29.8: ‘Friend Visākha, true knowledge is a counterpart of ignorance.’
mn44:29.9: ‘What is a counterpart of true knowledge, lady?’
mn44:29.10: ‘Friend Visākha, deliverance is a counterpart of true knowledge.’
mn44:29.11: ‘What is a counterpart of deliverance, lady?’
mn44:29.12: ‘Friend Visākha, Nibbāna is a counterpart of deliverance.’
mn44:29.13: ‘What is a counterpart of Nibbāna, lady?’
mn44:29.14: ‘Friend Visākha, you have pushed this line of questioning too far. You cannot find a conclusion to this line of questioning;
mn44:29.15: for it is the life divine that merges in Nibbāna, leads to Nibbāna.
mn44:29.16: If you like, you may go to the Blessed One and ask him the meaning of this. As he answers, so you should remember it.’
mn44:30.1: Then the lay follower Visākha delighted in the bhikkhuni Dhammadinnā’s words, and after agreeing, he rose from his seat, and after paying homage keeping her on his right, he departed and went to the Blessed One. After paying homage to him, he sat down at one side.
mn44:30.2: When he had done so, he recounted to the Blessed One all his conversation with the bhikkhuni Dhammadinnā.
mn44:30.3: When this was said, the Blessed One told him:
mn44:30.4: ‘The bhikkhuni Dhammadinnā is wise, Visākha, the bhikkhuni Dhammadinnā has great understanding.
mn44:30.5: Had you asked me the meaning of this, I should have given you the same reply.
mn44:30.6: As the bhikkhuni Dhammadinnā has answered you, such is the meaning, and so you should remember it.’
mn44:30.7: This is what the Blessed One said.
mn44:30.8: The lay follower Visākha was satisfied, and he delighted in the Blessed One’s words.
